acquisition.why: Inbound channels such as SEO, Amazon search, paid search and paid social can be largely agent-run. Ad creative and budgets still need human approval. The model depends on Amazon and Google.

delivery.why: Physical product: sourcing, QC, inventory, FBA or 3PL and returns all need human supplier management. Physical work caps this score.

billing.why: Shopify/Stripe or Amazon payouts run unattended.

support.why: Agents can answer where-is-my-order and FAQ queries. Returns, defects and Amazon account health need human checks.

scores.R_why: A £300 budget won't cover inventory, samples, branding and ads for a physical hero product [E: realistic minimum £2-5k]. UK product safety rules apply, plus food-contact rules for bottles. The keyword volumes quoted are US figures. Supplier negotiation and QC don't fit 6-8 h/week well. A dropship or print-on-demand variant could be tested cheaply.
scores.M_why: Low-difficulty keywords get found quickly in 2026. Amazon Basics and Chinese sellers undercut on price, and AI-generated brands flood the niches. Rare gaps exist but don't last.
scores.one_line: Inbound acquisition can be automated, but physical sourcing, capital needs beyond £300 and the hypothetical demo-style evidence (AI-imagined bottle brand, US keyword data) make this a poor agent-run fit.

acquisition.why: SEO and content for searches like 'website for artists' can be agent-produced, though ranking takes months. The validation stage involved social replies and outreach, and DMs to individuals would breach PECR, so only the inbound route counts.

onboarding.why: Self-serve signup and template choice. Agents can help migrate portfolios.

delivery.why: Hosted SaaS runs unattended once built. It still needs ongoing maintenance, uptime, domains and SSL.

support.why: Agents can handle how-to and DNS questions. Bugs and edge cases need Ricardo.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build an MVP, but a website builder is a large product (editor, hosting, domains, e-commerce for print sales) to build at 6-8 h/week. Artists have low willingness to pay. The £300 test is limited to a landing page and waitlist.
scores.M_why: Squarespace, Wix, Format, Pixpa, Cargo, Adobe Portfolio and Artwork Archive all serve artists already. AI site generators are commoditising the category. Search volume mostly goes to incumbents.
scores.one_line: A brainstormed idea from a single video, with no first-hand evidence, that faces entrenched incumbents and AI site generators. Unattractive despite being automatable SaaS.

acquisition.why: The proven routes are a personal network (texting friends), an existing audience and personal social media. Content or YouTube inbound is legal but founder-face dependent and slow to build. Cold DMs to individuals are banned under PECR.

onboarding.why: Payment, community invites and an intake questionnaire can all be automated.

delivery.why: The value comes from live calls, one-to-ones and daily comments by the founder (about 10 h/week per cohort). Self-paced content alone has low value.

support.why: Members expect the founder's personal answers.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has the technical skill to teach. But running a live cohort exceeds his 6-8 h/week and he has no audience. It is also the opposite of an agent-run business. A £300 test via a small cohort is feasible but trades time for money.
scores.M_why: 'Learn AI' cohorts and Skool communities are heavily saturated in 2026. Free YouTube and the AI tools themselves substitute. Only narrow vertical cohorts have room.
scores.one_line: Reasonably corroborated across 5 videos, but it is founder-delivered live teaching sold via personal network and audience, so it can't be agent-run and doesn't fit 6-8 h/week.

acquisition.why: Selling to contractors (B2B) in the UK means cold email to limited companies, which is legal. Many UK trades are sole traders, though, so they need TPS-screened calls or postal mail. Valpak-style lists and SMS to owners don't work in the UK. Homeowner postcards are legal by post but cost money per send.

onboarding.why: Contractors submit service area, offer and branding through a form. Agents set up campaigns with human checks.

delivery.why: The address, image, AI edit and print-API pipeline can be automated, but needs human QC of mockups for accuracy and misleading claims. UK Street View reuse likely breaches Google's terms. Physical mail is outsourced to a print API.

billing.why: Subscription or per-campaign Stripe billing. Revenue share on jobs would need attribution disputes resolved by a human.

support.why: Contractors will dispute lead quality and want account management.

scores.R_why: Technically buildable by Ricardo. However, there is no Zillow API in the UK, Google imagery terms block commercial reuse, addressed mail must handle UK GDPR legitimate-interest assessments, and fake-damage mockups risk breaching the CAP code and consumer protection rules. Postage and print alone could consume the £300 [E: roughly £1-1.50 per personalised card]. Most of the evidence is hypothetical riffing.
scores.M_why: Personalised AI direct mail for UK trades is still novel. However, it is easy to copy, and print-API vendors and CRMs will add the feature themselves.
scores.one_line: A clever automated pipeline, but data-source and Google terms are a problem in the UK, GDPR applies to addressed mail, sole-trader buyers are hard to reach legally, and the performance claims are hypothetical or second-hand.

acquisition.why: The proven channels are networking, a podcast and Facebook ads leading to sales calls. Paid ads are legal and could be agent-managed, but closing needs a human call. Cold email works only for limited companies, and many local trades are sole traders.

onboarding.why: Requires GBP access, verification, an audit call and gathering client assets.

delivery.why: White-label tools plus AI agents can handle posts, review requests, citations and LLM-friendly content. Human QA is needed, and results are uncertain.

billing.why: Stripe retainers; churn handling needs a human.

support.why: Local SMB owners want monthly reports and calls and will question ranking changes.

scores.R_why: A recurring-revenue service Ricardo can technically deliver with agents. A £300 Facebook-ads test is possible [E]. Sales calls and client management strain 6-8 h/week, but 3-5 clients is plausible. UK local SMB demand is real.
scores.M_why: Local SEO and GBP agencies are extremely crowded and cold-pitched to death. Google and AI tools (e.g. GBP auto-posts) erode the value. The 'AI search visibility' angle has temporary novelty.
scores.one_line: Feasible agent-assisted retainer with UK demand, but sales and account management stay human and the market is saturated. Margins depend on Ricardo selling.

acquisition.why: No scalable channel is evidenced; the examples came from first customers and existing relationships. Cold email to UK limited companies with inbound sales teams is legal, and content or SEO is possible. Selling implementations still needs discovery calls.

onboarding.why: Each client needs CRM and form integration, FAQ training, consent wording and testing. That is bespoke per client.

delivery.why: Once configured, it runs unattended: replies to inbound leads, qualifies and books. It needs monitoring for bad replies.

support.why: Agents can monitor logs and tweak prompts. Escalations go to a human.

scores.R_why: Well matched to Ricardo's technical skills. The build is cheap (Make, n8n, LLM APIs). Replying to inbound enquiries is PECR-compliant, though UK GDPR, AI disclosure and call-recording rules apply. The bottleneck is selling and per-client setup within 6-8 h/week.
scores.M_why: Very crowded in 2026: GoHighLevel, HubSpot AI agents, Intercom Fin, CRM-native features and countless AI-automation agencies. Differentiating requires a vertical niche (e.g. UK venues or clinics).
scores.one_line: Real ROI with first-hand corroboration and a good technical fit, but it is a commoditising, crowded AI-agency service with bespoke onboarding and human-led sales.

acquisition.why: Marketplaces (Etsy, Gumroad), SEO and Pinterest provide inbound that agents can run. The described community DMs to individuals are a PECR risk, and community posts must follow group rules. Depends on marketplace platforms.

delivery.why: Agents can draft the product. Ricardo approves quality once, then delivery is automatic.

support.why: Download issues and refunds can be handled by agents.

scores.R_why: Fits £300, 6-8 h/week and an agent workflow well. UK VAT on digital sales is handled by the marketplace (Etsy/Gumroad as merchant of record), and pre-sales need refund terms. The main challenge is finding demand without an audience.
scores.M_why: Templates and kits are flooded by AI-generated products, and buyers can ask ChatGPT for the same content. Only very narrow pain-specific niches have headroom, with low prices and low revenue per item.
scores.one_line: Cheap, legal and highly automatable to test, but revenue per product is low and generic kits are being commoditised by AI. The '18 pre-sales' claim relies on an existing audience Ricardo doesn't have.

acquisition.why: Horizontal no-code agent SaaS needs heavy content and paid marketing spend. An affiliate channel is mentioned only once. Inbound SEO is technically legal but hopeless against funded incumbents.

onboarding.why: Self-serve with templates, but users need hand-holding to build working agents.

delivery.why: The software runs itself. Reliability, integrations and LLM costs need constant engineering.

support.why: Agent-debugging support is heavy and technical.

scores.R_why: Building a Lindy or Zapier competitor needs a full-time funded team and integration breadth. That is impossible at 6-8 h/week and £300.
scores.M_why: Lindy, Zapier Agents, n8n, Make, Gumbo, OpenAI and Google agent builders are saturating the market. Frontier labs ship this natively, so a solo entrant has essentially no room.
scores.one_line: The evidence is a vendor talk (Lindy feature claims), not a business case. A crowded horizontal platform that a solo part-timer cannot build or compete with.
